title: Mutual zugzwang and mined squares
summary: Positions where the side to move loses, and the squares a king must not step on first.
part.halfPoint.title: Half a point
part.halfPoint.summary: In Hooper's position, the wrong side to move only loses the win.
part.trebuchet.title: The trébuchet
part.trebuchet.summary: Two blocked pawns, two attacking kings: whoever has the move loses. And how Lasker got there.
part.mined.title: Mined squares
part.mined.summary: The square your king must not step on first, and how to make the other king step on his.
part.defend.title: The zugzwang that saves
part.defend.summary: On the weaker side, the same squares hold the draw and even set a trap.
part.alekhine.title: Wait next to the mine
part.alekhine.summary: Alekhine waits one square away until the black king steps on his own.
part.noMine.title: When the mine does not decide
part.noMine.summary: If the defender protects the pawn from another square, it is a draw.
part.recap.title: The technique and the summary
part.recap.summary: The mined-square technique in another structure, three rules and the key position to play.
step.t_hooper: King and pawn against king: the pawn is already on the seventh, protected by the king on b6, and the black king stands in front of it. This is Hooper's example of mutual zugzwang. What happens with Black to move? And if it were White's move?
step.t_hooper.hint1: Count the black king's squares: the c7-pawn attacks b8 and d8.
step.t_hooper.hint2: With White to move, the white king either abandons the pawn or takes away the black king's last square.
step.hooper: With Black to move, 1...Kd7 is the only move, because the pawn attacks b8 and d8; and 2.Kb7 takes the pawn to a queen. With White to move, 1.Kc6 stalemates the black king, and any other move abandons c7: a draw. Both sides are in zugzwang, but here the wrong side to move does not lose the game, it only loses the win. It is half a point. Soon you will see the form where it costs the whole point.
step.d_hooper: Black to move: see why Black loses.
step.d_hooper.m1: 1...Kd7: the only move, because b8 and d8 are attacked by the pawn.
step.d_hooper.m2: 2.Kb7: my king covers c8, and nothing can stop the pawn.
step.d_hooper.m3: 2...Kd6: the black king can neither take on c7 nor go to c8, because my king controls both squares.
step.d_hooper.m4: 3.c8=Q. With White to move in that position, none of this would exist.
step.hooperMove: White to play and win. The pawn is still on the sixth, and your king is already next to it. Reach Hooper's position with Black to move.
step.hooperMove.hint: Compare with Hooper's position: one piece still has to reach its square, and it is not the king.
step.hooperMove.done: Right. 1.d7! set up Hooper's position with Black to move: 1...Ke7 was the only move, and 2.Kc7 covers d8. With a king move, it would have been your move there, and only a draw.
step.t_treb: In Hooper's position the wrong side to move only lost the win. Here both pawns are blocked, and each king protects its own pawn and attacks the other one. What happens with Black to move? And with White to move?
step.t_treb.hint1: No pawn can move. Whoever has the move can only move the king.
step.t_treb.hint2: If the black king leaves c4, who protects the d5-pawn? And if the white king leaves e5, who protects d4?
step.treb: Here nobody wants to move. The pawns cannot move, so the side to move has to move the king and abandon its own pawn. With Black to move, my king takes on d5 and stands in front of my pawn; with White to move, it is the black king that takes d4. This position is called the trébuchet, the catapult of medieval sieges (trébucher, in French, means to stumble). It is a full-point mutual zugzwang: the wrong side to move loses the game.
step.d_treb: Look at the trébuchet with Black to move. I play both sides.
step.d_treb.m1: 1...Kb4: the black king has to step away, and any square abandons the d5-pawn.
step.d_treb.m2: 2.Kxd5. The black pawn is gone, and my king stands in front of my pawn.
step.d_treb.m3: 2...Kb5: the black king tries to come back, but my king already stands in front of the pawn and still protects it.
step.d_treb.m4: 3.Kd6: d6 is a key square of the d4-pawn. The pawn will queen.
step.trebMove: White to play and win. Build the trébuchet with Black to move, then collect the pawn.
step.trebMove.hint: Your king must protect d4 and attack d5 at the same time. Only one square does both.
step.trebMove.done: Right. 1.Ke5 closed the trébuchet with Black to move, and the d5-pawn was left without defence. Any other first move would have lost the d4-pawn.
step.lasker: This happened in a simultaneous exhibition in Philadelphia, in 1892. Emanuel Lasker, who would become world champion in 1894, had Black against H. G. Voigt. After a long game, rook and f4-pawn were left against bishop and g2-pawn, and the white king has just come to g4 to attack the pawn. With the bishop on f3 in the way, the rook does not win by itself. Lasker saw something else: a trébuchet around f3 and f4, with White to move.
step.laskerMove: Now you are Lasker. Black to play and win.
step.laskerMove.hint: Which white piece stands in the way of the trébuchet around f3 and f4? A rook is worth less than the game.
step.laskerMove.done: 81...Rxf3! 82.gxf3 Ke3: the trébuchet with White to move. The king on g4 has to step away and abandon f3, and the f4-pawn marches on to queen. Lasker gave back the rook just to get the right side to move, and the game ended there, 0-1.
step.t_mined: In the trébuchet the kings were already in place. Here they still have to arrive, and whoever reaches his square first loses. This is the key position of the lesson: the pawns are blocked on d5 and d6, your king wants to take d6 and the black king wants to take d5. Which way does the white king go, and which square must it not step on?
step.t_mined.hint1: Look for the squares where the two kings would form a trébuchet around d5 and d6.
step.t_mined.hint2: White king on e6 and black king on c5: a trébuchet. Whoever reaches his square first hands the move to the other side.
step.t_mined.hint3: Do not step on e6 now. Look for another square from which your king attacks d6.
step.mines: Look at the two marked squares. If my king steps on e6 and Black answers with c5, we have a trébuchet with White to move, and I lose. If the black king steps on c5 and I answer with e6, the trébuchet is his. That is why e6 is called a mined square for the white king, and c5 for the black king: whoever steps on it first blows up. When there is only one pair of such squares, the books call them mined squares.
step.trap: See what happens if I step first: 1.Ke6? and the black king answers 1...Kc5. Now it is my move. My king has to leave e6, the d5-pawn falls, and Black wins. The mine was mine.
step.d_mined: The right way: attack d6 from a square that is not mined.
step.d_mined.m1: 1.Kf6! The white king heads for e7, which also attacks d6, without stepping on e6.
step.d_mined.m2: 1...Kb5: the black king comes closer, but he has not stepped on c5 yet.
step.d_mined.m3: 2.Ke7: now the d6-pawn is attacked. Black has to protect it.
step.d_mined.m4: 2...Kc5: only c5 protects d6 in time, and the black king steps on his own mined square.
step.d_mined.m5: 3.Ke6, and now stepping here is good: the black king got there first, and the trébuchet is set with Black to move.
step.d_mined.m6: 3...Kb6: in the trébuchet with the move, the black king has to step away and abandon d6.
step.minedMove: White to play and win. Follow Viktor's path: attack d6 without stepping on the mine first.
step.minedMove.hint: Go through f6 and e7. Step on e6 only after the black king is on c5.
step.minedMove.done: Perfect. The black king had to step on c5 to defend d6, and only then did you enter e6. Black is in zugzwang.
step.t_defend: Now you defend. Black is better: the black king is close to the pawns. Which is the only square that saves the draw?
step.t_defend.hint1: Look for the trébuchet around d3 and d4. Which are the two mined squares?
step.t_defend.hint2: The mines are c4 for your king and e3 for Black's. If the black king steps on e3, yours must reach c4 on the next move.
step.defend: The mines here are c4 for my king and e3 for the black king. If I step on c4 first, Black comes to e3 and I lose. So I wait with 1.Kb4, right next to c4. Now the black king cannot go to e3 either: I would answer 2.Kc4 and it would be his move. Every other move loses: 1.Kc4 steps on the mine, and the rest leave the white king too far away to answer 1...Ke3 with 2.Kc4.
step.defendTrap: The mistake that looks natural: 1.Kc4?, attacking the d4-pawn. Black answers 1...Ke3, and it is my move in the trébuchet. My king has to abandon d3. The mine was on c4.
step.d_defend: And if Black is careless, the zugzwang changes sides.
step.d_defend.m1: 1.Kb4! The white king waits next to the mine.
step.d_defend.m2: 1...Ke3? Black steps on e3, his own mine, and hands me the move in the wrong place for him.
step.d_defend.m3: 2.Kc4: the trébuchet with Black to move.
step.d_defend.m4: 2...Kf3: in the trébuchet with the move, the black king has to abandon d4.
step.d_defend.m5: 3.Kxd4. The defender is now the one who wins.
step.defendMove: White to play and draw. Pick the right waiting square and answer the black king.
step.defendMove.hint: Wait next to c4, without stepping on it. When the black king moves away from d4, attack the pawn.
step.defendMove.done: Excellent. After 1.Kb4 Kf3, 2.Kc5 attacked d4: to defend the pawn the black king would have to step on e3, and you would answer 3.Kc4. 2.Kc5 was the only move, and now you are the one playing for the win.
step.t_alekhine: Alekhine against Yates, Hamburg, 1910. Alekhine traded the rooks with 40.Re5 Rxe5 41.fxe5, and after 43.e4 f4 the central pawns were blocked on e4 and f4, on neighbouring files. On the queenside only the a3 and a4 pawns are blocked; the b-pawns can still move. The e5-pawn is White's, but the black king is going to take it. Where are the mines, and what does White play?
step.t_alekhine.hint1: On which square does the white king protect e4 and attack f4? And the black king, after taking on e5?
step.t_alekhine.hint2: The mines are f3 for the white king and e5 for Black's. Black will want to take on e5: let him step first.
step.alekhine: If my king steps on f3 right away, 45.Kf3? Kxe5 sets up the trébuchet with me to move: the king has to abandon e4, and Black wins. Waiting with a pawn does not work either: 45.b3? axb3 loses. Alekhine played 45.Kf2!, next to the mine. After 45...Kxe5 the black king had stepped on his, and 46.Kf3 left Yates in the trébuchet with the move. The b-pawns gave him no waiting move: 46...b4 47.axb4 would only leave White another passed pawn. The game ended there, 1-0.
step.d_alekhine: The same position without the b-pawns, which do not change the count. And what if Black does not take on e5?
step.d_alekhine.m1: 1.Kf2! I wait next to f3, without stepping on it.
step.d_alekhine.m2: 1...Kd7: Black does not want to step on e5.
step.d_alekhine.m3: 2.Kf3: with the black king far from e5, f3 is no longer a mine, and now I attack f4.
step.d_alekhine.m4: 2...Ke6: too late, because from e6 the black king does not protect f4.
step.d_alekhine.m5: 3.Kxf4: the pawn is gone, and my e4-pawn has the king beside it.
step.alekhineMove: White to play and win. Now Black is going to take on e5. Do as Alekhine did.
step.alekhineMove.hint: Stay next to your mine until the black king steps on his.
step.alekhineMove.done: Right. 1.Kf2 Kxe5 2.Kf3: Black is in the trébuchet with the move, like Yates in the game.
step.t_noMine: So far someone was forced to step on his mine. Now the scene moves to the other wing: the f4 and f5 pawns are the ones from the trébuchet, but the kings are far away. Your king wants to take f5, and Black's wants to take f4. Where are the mines, and can White win?
step.t_noMine.hint1: The trébuchet here would have the white king on e5 and the black king on g4.
step.t_noMine.hint2: To defend f5, does the black king really need g4? Look for another square, one the f4-pawn does not attack.
step.noMine: The mines are e5 for me and g4 for Black: 1.Ke5? Kg4 and it is my move. Too far away loses as well: 1.Kc4? Kg4, and my king does not get back in time to defend f4. But I cannot force Black onto g4 either, because he defends f5 from g6, a square the f4-pawn does not attack. If he stepped on g4 early, 1.Kd5 Kg4? 2.Ke5! would win. When the defender has a square like that, the mine does not decide: do not step on yours and accept the draw.
step.d_noMine: See the best play for both sides.
step.d_noMine.m1: 1.Kd5: I stay close to e5, without stepping on it.
step.d_noMine.m2: 1...Kg6: the black king defends f5 from g6, far from his mine.
step.d_noMine.m3: 2.Ke6: now I attack f5, and g6 keeps defending it.
step.d_noMine.m4: 2...Kg7! Black gives up f5, but the king heads for the square in front of my pawn.
step.d_noMine.m5: 3.Kxf5: I take the pawn Black gave up.
step.d_noMine.m6: 3...Kf7: the black king stands in front of the pawn, in opposition. The f4-pawn cannot get through: it is a draw.
step.noMineMove: White to play and draw. Do not step on your mine, and do not wander too far either.
step.noMineMove.hint: e5 is your mine; c3, c4 and c5 are too far from f4.
step.noMineMove.done: Right. You did not step on e5 while the black king could answer on g4, and did not wander too far from f4. And the black king, which defends f5 from g6 and then heads for the square in front of the pawn, never has to step on g4: the mine does not decide, and it is a draw.
step.t_race: To finish, the mined-square technique in another structure: pawns on e5 and e6, the white king on c7 and the black king on g4. Where are the mined squares, and which way does your king go?
step.t_race.hint1: The kings form a trébuchet around e5 and e6 with White on d6 and Black on f5.
step.t_race.hint2: 1.Kd6 right away steps on the mine. Look for a square from which your king attacks e6 and is not mined.
step.race: The mines: d6 for the white king, f5 for the black king. If I step on d6 first, 1.Kd6? Kf5! and it is my move in the trébuchet. But from d7 my king also attacks e6, and d7 is not mined. Black has to defend the pawn, and only f5 does that. Black steps on the mine, I enter d6, and it is Black's move.
step.d_race: Watch how Black is forced to step on f5.
step.d_race.m1: 1.Kd7! Attacks e6 from a safe square.
step.d_race.m2: 1...Kf5: the black king defends the pawn from the only square it can, f5, his own mine.
step.d_race.m3: 2.Kd6: now it works. The trébuchet is set and it is Black's move.
step.d_race.m4: 2...Kg5: in the trébuchet with the move, the black king has to let go of e6.
step.d_race.m5: 3.Kxe6. The e5-pawn is free, with the king beside it.
step.raceMove: White to play and win. Attack e6 without stepping on the mine.
step.raceMove.hint: Your king goes to d7. If Black does not defend e6, take it.
step.raceMove.done: Well done. Black refused to step on f5, and the e6-pawn fell at once. Had he gone to f5, you would have entered d6.
step.rules: Three rules to take with you. First: with blocked pawns, look for the trébuchet; the side to move there loses the game, and in Hooper's position it loses half a point. Second: do not step on your mine first; attack the pawn from another square, or wait next to the mine until the other king steps on his, like Alekhine. Third: the mine only decides if the other king needs his; if he defends the pawn from another square, it is a draw.
step.finish: Now play the key position to the end. Do not step on e6 too early.
ex.e08: White to play and draw. The g4 and g5 pawns are blocked, and pushing b5 or c5 gives the pawn away: only the kings play.
ex.e08.hint: The g4 and g5 pawns cannot move. Look at the trébuchet around b5 and c5: where are the mines?
ex.e08.solution: 1.Kd3 holds (so does 1.Kb3). The mines are c4 for the white king and b6 for Black's. 1.Kc4? loses: after 1...Kb6 it is White's move and there is no pawn move to wait with. 1.b6? loses too. If the black king steps on b6 first, 2.Kc4 is the answer.
ex.e10: White to play and win. Take the pawn, then mind the mine.
ex.e10.hint: After taking on c6, the white king heads for e5. Which square around e4 and e5 is your mine?
ex.e10.solution: 1.Kxc6, and after 1...Kg4, 2.Kd6! (2.Kd5? steps on the mine: 2...Kf4 and it is White's move). When the black king comes to f4, 3.Kd5 closes the trébuchet with Black to move. Every move in this line is the only one that wins.
ex.e11: White to play and win. No blocked pawns, but a mutual zugzwang is hiding here.
ex.e11.hint: With the white king on b6, the pawn on c7 and the black king on c8, the side to move misses out. Who do you want to be on move?
ex.e11.solution: 1.Kb6! reaches that position with Black to move: 1...Kd7 is the only move, and 2.Kb7 takes the pawn to a queen. It is a mutual zugzwang: with White to move there, it would be a draw, because 1.Kc6 is stalemate and any other move lets the black king take the pawn. 1.Ka5, 1.Kb5 and 1.Ka7 only draw.
ex.e13: White to play and draw. The blocked pawns are further back, on c3 and c4.
ex.e13.hint: The trébuchet here would have your king on d4 and Black's on b3. Which of the two squares is yours?
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kd5 holds (so does 1.Ke4). 1.Kd4? steps on the mine: 1...Kb3 and White, to move, abandons c3. And why is there no win? After 1.Kd5, the black king defends c4 from b5, a square that is not mined. When the defender has such a square, the mine does not decide.
key.trebuchet: Each king attacks the other's pawn, and neither can take because its own pawn is defended. The side to move has to step away, losing its pawn and the game.
key.mined: Each king has its own mine here, the square beside the enemy pawn: e6 for the white king, c5 for the black one. Whoever steps on his first walks into a trébuchet with the move and loses.
key.race: The white king attacks the black pawn from above, without stepping on the mine beside it. That way it is the black king that runs out of good squares.
key.cheeseman: Each king captures a pawn on its own wing and heads back to the centre. On the way back, whoever reaches the mined square first loses: you have to stop one square short.
key.lasker: Lasker gives back his rook to reach the position where the side to move loses, and the side that has to move is his opponent. Simultaneous exhibition in Philadelphia, 1892.
key.alekhine: Alekhine waits one square away from the mined square; when the black king takes the pawn, he steps in and leaves him without good moves. Hamburg, 1910.
history: Zugzwang is a German word meaning the compulsion to move. Pawn endings have a curious feature: positions where the side to move loses, whoever that is. This is mutual zugzwang, and it decides far more games than you might think. Its harshest form is named after a medieval weapon, the trébuchet, a kind of catapult; the French verb it comes from, trébucher, means to stumble, which is exactly what happens to the king. The idea is ancient: there are zugzwang problems in shatranj, the Arabic forerunner of chess, more than a thousand years old. Mined squares are the other side of the coin: squares your king must not step on first, because doing so hands the zugzwang to the opponent. Mark Dvoretsky, one of the greatest trainers in history, gave them a section of his endgame manual. And they decide real games: Emanuel Lasker, in a simultaneous exhibition in Philadelphia in 1892, gave back a rook just to reach this position with his opponent to move; and Alexander Alekhine beat Frederick Yates in Hamburg, in 1910, because he did not step on the mined square first.
practice: Now the real endgame: the key position, with you to move. Remember where your mine is. Pick the time control and go.
